title: Short Stuff: Dare Stones
summary: Short Stuff follow-up to the Roanoke Colony episode, focused on the Dare Stones. Recaps the 1587 English colony at Roanoke, the John White return to find the colony gone and the word CROATOAN carved on a tree, and the mystery that followed. In 1937 Lewis Hammond (a California produce dealer) showed Emory University a white quartzite stone inscribed with a message attributed to Eleanor White Dare, which professors Heywood J. Pierce Jr. and Heywood J. Pierce Sr. (of Brenau University) publicized. Investigators could not verify Hammond or relocate the find site. A $5 reward for more stones led stone cutter Bill Eberhardt to supply 42 forgeries, paid $2,000. The Saturday Evening Post in April 1941 exposed the stones as a hoax, citing anachronisms such as Arabic numerals and vs. spelling. Some still argue the first Hammond stone may be authentic, citing its unusual stone and expert opinion on medieval graffiti, and hope modern testing will settle it.

segments.title: Opening and follow-up setup
segments.summary: The hosts introduce this short follow-up to the Roanoke Colony episode, noting the Dare Stones got only a few minutes there and need more detail.

segments.title: Roanoke background and the missing colonists
segments.summary: The 1587 colony led by John White, with his daughter Eleanor Dare and granddaughter Virginia Dare, is recalled. White returns from England after three years to find the colony gone and CROATOAN carved on a tree, with no cross. The fate of the colonists remains unknown, and rumors reached Jamestown settlers without confirmation.

segments.title: Lewis Hammond's stone at Emory
segments.summary: In 1937 Lewis Hammond, a California produce dealer on a hickory nut trip in North Carolina, brought an inscribed stone to Emory University. The translated message, attributed to Eleanor White Dare, describes deaths, a slain child and son-in-law, and a burial near a hill. Hammond could not relocate the spot and sold the stone, then left.

segments.title: Pierce professors, reward, and Bill Eberhardt's forgeries
segments.summary: Heywood J. Pierce Jr. published a paper on the stone. Investigators could not verify Hammond. A five-dollar reward for more stones prompted stone cutter Bill Eberhardt to supply 42 stones, paid $2,000, which together told a fictional story of Eleanor's later life in Georgia.

segments.title: Saturday Evening Post exposé and the hoax verdict
segments.summary: In April 1941 the Saturday Evening Post published an article exposing the stones as forgeries, pointing to anachronisms such as Arabic numerals and vs. spelling. Brenau University suffered public embarrassment and the stones were hidden away.

segments.title: Authenticity debate and sign-off
segments.summary: Some still argue the original Hammond stone may be real, citing its white quartzite and expert analysis of medieval graffiti, and hope modern testing will settle it. The hosts sign off and point to the Roanoke episode and a HowStuffWorks article.
